clinicalPearls: The most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by a quantitative or qualitative defect in von Willebrand factor, which mediates platelet adhesion and carries and stabilises factor VIII
The bleeding pattern is that of primary haemostatic failure: mucocutaneous bleeding with easy bruising, epistaxis, menorrhagia, and prolonged bleeding after dental or surgical procedures
Type 1 is a partial quantitative deficiency (most common and usually mild), type 2 comprises qualitative variants, and type 3 is a severe near-complete deficiency with the heaviest bleeding
Because von Willebrand factor protects factor VIII, low levels can produce a modestly prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time alongside normal platelet count
Diagnosis relies on measuring von Willebrand factor antigen, its functional (ristocetin cofactor or equivalent) activity, and factor VIII, with multimer analysis to subtype
Factor levels fluctuate with stress, pregnancy, oestrogens, and inflammation, so borderline results may need repeat testing
Desmopressin releases stored von Willebrand factor and is useful in type 1 and many type 2 cases but is ineffective or inappropriate in type 3 and certain subtypes

When desmopressin is unsuitable, von Willebrand factor-containing concentrates and antifibrinolytic agents are the mainstays for bleeding or procedures; an acquired form can occur with other disorders
reference.pathophysiology: Von Willebrand factor is a large multimeric glycoprotein synthesised by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes. It bridges platelets to exposed subendothelial collagen at sites of vascular injury (particularly under high shear) and serves as the carrier that protects circulating factor VIII from degradation. In VWD, reduced quantity (types 1 and 3) or impaired function (type 2 variants) of this factor impairs platelet adhesion and aggregation, and the loss of factor VIII protection lowers its level, adding a secondary coagulation defect. The result is defective primary haemostasis with a mucocutaneous bleeding phenotype. Acquired von Willebrand syndrome can arise from adsorption onto abnormal cells, high shear (e.g. aortic stenosis), or autoantibodies.
additionalDifferentials: Platelet function disorders (e.g. Glanzmann thrombasthenia, storage pool disease)
Immune thrombocytopenia and other causes of thrombocytopenia
Vascular/connective tissue causes of mucocutaneous bleeding
Vitamin K deficiency or liver disease affecting coagulation
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film to assess platelet number and morphology
Coagulation screen including activated partial thromboplastin time
Von Willebrand factor antigen level and functional (ristocetin cofactor/collagen-binding) activity
Von Willebrand factor multimer analysis and ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation to define subtype
Repeat testing when results are borderline, accounting for stress, pregnancy, and hormonal influences
redFlags: Severe or life-threatening haemorrhage, including gastrointestinal or intracranial bleeding, particularly in type 3 disease
Uncontrolled menorrhagia causing haemodynamic compromise or severe anaemia
Major unplanned surgery or trauma in a patient with a significant factor deficiency
New or worsening bleeding suggesting acquired von Willebrand syndrome linked to another disease
reference.prognosis: Most patients, especially those with type 1 disease, have a mild course and a normal life expectancy with appropriate peri-procedural planning; type 3 and severe type 2 disease carry a higher lifelong bleeding burden but are manageable with modern replacement and adjunctive therapy.
pitfalls: Excluding VWD on the basis of a normal activated partial thromboplastin time or normal platelet count
Missing the diagnosis because factor levels are transiently normalised by stress, pregnancy, or oestrogen use
Giving desmopressin in type 2B (which can worsen thrombocytopenia) or in type 3 (where it is ineffective)
Overlooking acquired von Willebrand syndrome in older patients or those with lymphoproliferative, myeloproliferative, or cardiac conditions
Failing to plan replacement or antifibrinolytic cover before invasive procedures
management: Use desmopressin to release endogenous von Willebrand factor for bleeding or minor procedures in type 1 and responsive type 2 disease, after confirming response with a therapeutic trial
Give von Willebrand factor-containing concentrate for type 3, severe type 2, major bleeding or major surgery where desmopressin is ineffective or unsuitable
Add the antifibrinolytic tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding, epistaxis, dental extraction and menorrhagia
Control menorrhagia with hormonal measures such as the combined oral contraceptive or a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system alongside haemostatic therapy
Avoid antiplatelet agents and NSAIDs, and plan peri-procedural haemostatic cover in advance
Provide genetic counselling for autosomal recessive type 3 and family testing, with patient education and a medical-alert record
Manage through a specialist haemophilia or haematology centre with an individualised bleeding-management plan
